model.name: Plan / Schedule
model.purpose: Represent intentions bound to time: what an agent intends to do, how firmly, when, in what order, under which commitments, and how the intention was later revised or realized.
model.scope_statement: This model is the composite root for a plan: an identified, versioned statement of intention held by an agent, together with the planned actions it contains, their binding to instants, intervals, deadlines and recurrence patterns, the ordering and date constraints among them, the commitments that make some intentions binding on third parties, and the baselines, change records, progress and realization links that let intention be compared with what happened. It is deliberately independent of storage and interface: iCalendar, JSCalendar, a Gantt tool file, a Git-tracked Markdown plan or a MongoDB document are projections of the same semantics. It does not own agent identity, act records, process definitions or cost measurement.
in_scope: Plan identity, classification, intent strength, version and supersession
Planned actions with preconditions, expected effects and effort estimates
Binding of intended actions to instants, intervals, deadlines, durations and recurrence patterns, including time zone and floating-time semantics
Ordering dependencies, lag, date constraints, and the dates, float and critical path derived from them
Resource and participant assignment, availability and contention
Commitments binding an agent to a beneficiary, with consequences, remedies and release
Baselines, change logs, progress actuals, variance, realization links and plan closure
Disclosure level, access grants, provenance and retention of plan and schedule records
out_of_scope: Completed acts and their observations, owned by the act/action model
Standing process or workflow definitions, which are types rather than dated intentions
Agent identity, roles and organizational structure
Cost estimates, budgets and earned-value measurement
Calendar transport, storage and synchronization protocols (CalDAV, JMAP, iTIP bindings) as engineering surfaces
Motion planning and robot trajectory generation
Contract formation and enforcement beyond binding an intention to a beneficiary

boundary_notes.distinction: A task is an assignable unit of work with its own lifecycle and assignee; it references the plan that authorizes it. The plan is versioned independently, so a task state change does not revise the plan. JSCalendar keeps Event and Task as distinct object types for the same reason.

An act is a completed occurrence with observation evidence; a planned action is an intention that may never occur. PROV models this as an Activity that used a Plan, keeping plan and activity as separate entities rather than states of one thing.
A process definition is a reusable type with no dates; a plan is a dated instance of intention that may instantiate such a definition. Recurrence rules belong here, process step definitions do not.

A project is an endeavour with governance, funding and deliverables; its integrated schedule and baselines are bound from this model rather than redefined. GAO treats schedule assessment and cost estimating as linked but separate bodies of guidance.
A calendar is a container and access surface. Agenda, Gantt and busy-only views are projections of plan semantics; disclosure class and transparency are modelled here, the serving protocol is not.
Only the binding of an intention to a named beneficiary is in scope, aligned to an ODRL Duty within an Agreement. Contract formation, consideration and enforcement remain external.
Zone identifiers and their rules are referenced from the IANA database and never copied into the model; only the identifier and the database release in force are recorded.

sources.title: RFC 5545: Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
sources.relevance: Normative source for schedule entry components, STATUS values, DTSTART time forms (UTC, TZID local, floating, date-only), RRULE, RDATE, EXDATE, RECURRENCE-ID with RANGE, RELATED-TO, SEQUENCE, TRANSP, CLASS, PRIORITY, PERCENT-COMPLETE and VFREEBUSY.

sources.title: RFC 5546: iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP)
sources.relevance: Normative source for Organizer/Attendee authority, PARTSTAT response states, COUNTER and DECLINECOUNTER negotiation, and conflict resolution by UID then SEQUENCE then DTSTAMP.

sources.title: RFC 8984: JSCalendar: A JSON Representation of Calendar Data
sources.relevance: Normative source for Event/Task/Group typing, mandatory uid and updated, sequence, start/duration/due/estimatedDuration, timeZone and floating LocalDateTime, recurrenceRules and recurrenceOverrides, participants, progress, privacy and freeBusyStatus; mandates RFC 3339 form for UTC timestamps.

sources.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
sources.relevance: Normative timestamp profile of ISO 8601: mandatory fields, explicit numeric offset or Z, seconds including leap-second value 60, and the distinct meaning of -00:00 for unknown local offset.

sources.title: RFC 9557: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps with Additional Information
sources.relevance: Defines IXDTF bracketed suffix tags so an IANA time zone name travels with an RFC 3339 timestamp, redefines Z as 'UTC known, local offset unknown', and specifies handling when a stored offset conflicts with a critical time zone tag.

sources.title: Time Zone Database (tz / zoneinfo)
sources.relevance: Authoritative registry of time zone identifiers and historical and future offset and daylight-saving rules; release 2026c records Alberta moving to permanent -06 and Morocco to permanent +00, demonstrating that stored future local times can be invalidated by a data release.

sources.title: PROV-O: The PROV Ontology
sources.relevance: Normative treatment of prov:Plan as the plan an agent intended to follow, exposed through prov:qualifiedAssociation and prov:hadPlan, plus wasAssociatedWith, wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom and wasAttributedTo for plan provenance and the plan-to-activity link.

sources.title: Time Ontology in OWL
sources.relevance: Formal vocabulary for Instant, Interval, ProperInterval, Duration, DateTimeDescription, temporal reference systems via hasTRS, Allen interval relations for ordering, and inXSDDateTimeStamp where the time zone field is mandatory. Not yet a Recommendation, so cited as alignment only.

sources.title: ODRL Information Model 2.2
sources.relevance: Normative model for Duty and Obligation, Agreement between assigner and assignee, constraints as conditions on a rule, consequence for unfulfilled duties and remedy for infringed prohibitions; used to align commitment terms rather than inventing an obligation vocabulary.

sources.title: FHIR ValueSet: RequestIntent
sources.relevance: Published gradient of intentional authority: proposal (no authorization), plan (intention without authorizing others), directive, order and its order sub-kinds, and option; supplies an evidenced classifier for how firmly an intention binds.

sources.title: FHIR Data Types (Timing)
sources.relevance: An independent, non-iCalendar recurrence grammar (repeat with bounds, count, duration, frequency, period, dayOfWeek, timeOfDay, when, offset) used as a counterexample showing that recurrence models are not isomorphic and round-tripping is lossy.

sources.title: GAO Schedule Assessment Guide: Best Practices for Project Schedules (GAO-16-89G)
sources.relevance: Public-authority statement that a reliable schedule is comprehensive, well-constructed, credible and controlled, expressed as ten best practices: capturing all activities, sequencing all activities, assigning resources, establishing durations, horizontal and vertical traceability, a valid critical path, reasonable total float, schedule risk analysis, updating with actual progress and logic, and maintaining a baseline schedule.

sources.title: General Records Schedule 5.1: Common Office Records
sources.organization: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
sources.version_or_date: GRS 5.1, Transmittal No. 28 (July 2017) and subsequent transmittals
sources.relevance: Evidence that calendars and schedules of daily activities are scheduled records with authorized disposition: GRS 5.1 covers those of non-high-level officials, while high-level officials' records are addressed under GRS 6.1, establishing that retention of schedule data is role-dependent, not uniform.

sources.title: Schedule (schema.org type)
sources.relevance: A third recurrence grammar (repeatFrequency, repeatCount, byDay, byMonth, byMonthDay, byMonthWeek, scheduleTimezone, exceptDate, duration) attached to Event via eventSchedule; used for the public-publication projection and to evidence divergence between recurrence vocabularies.

sources.title: PDDL2.1: An Extension to PDDL for Expressing Temporal Planning Domains
sources.organization: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research (Fox and Long)
sources.relevance: Reference semantics for machine planning: durative actions with duration constraints and conditions annotated at-start, over-all and at-end, plus preconditions and effects, grounding the planned-action structure used by autonomous planning agents.

sources.title: RFC 5545: Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
sources.relevance: Primary calendaring object specification; aligned for calendar component, recurrence, free-busy, classification, attendee and identity properties. Recurrence expansion ambiguities are recorded as conflicts, not hidden.

sources.title: RFC 9253: Support for iCalendar Relationships
sources.relevance: Primary source for project-style temporal relations on calendar components: precedence types, GAP lead and lag, REFID grouping and LINK.

sources.title: PROV-O: The PROV Ontology
sources.relevance: Defines Plan as an entity and the association hadPlan; aligned for attribution, revision, generation and invalidation of plan versions.

sources.title: PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model
sources.relevance: Defines Plan as actions or steps intended by agents to achieve goals but leaves step structure to extensions; aligned for plan-as-entity, revision, generation and invalidation.

sources.title: Time Ontology in OWL
sources.relevance: Primary temporal topology vocabulary and the source of non-Gregorian TRS support beyond CALSCALE; aligned for Instant, ProperInterval, duration and Allen interval relations.

sources.title: The P-PLAN Ontology
sources.organization: Ontology Engineering Group, Universidad Politecnica de Madrid, and Information Sciences Institute, University of Southern California
sources.relevance: Primary scientific extension that structures plans into Steps and Variables and links them to execution traces; aligned for isPreceededBy, correspondsToStep and correspondsToVariable.

sources.title: HL7 FHIR CarePlan (Release 4)
sources.relevance: Primary instance-level care-intention resource; aligned for status and intent strength, partOf, basedOn, replaces and activity references. PlanDefinition remains out of scope.

sources.title: ISO 21502:2020 Project, programme and portfolio management - Guidance on project management
sources.relevance: Catalogue-level guidance treating schedule as structuring work, estimating durations, sequencing activities and maintaining a credible schedule baseline. Full text is paywalled, so baseline naming is an alignment with an evidence gap.

bundles.rationale: Calendaring standards make a globally unique identifier and a modification timestamp mandatory and resolve replica conflicts by identifier, revision counter and timestamp; FHIR publishes an evidenced gradient of intentional authority. Identity and authority must therefore be settled before any temporal or content claim can be relied on.

bundles.name: Network, Feasibility and Integrity
bundles.description: Ordering between intended items, imposed date constraints, the dates derived from them, resource feasibility and whether the result is fit to rely on.
bundles.rationale: GAO's ten best practices require that all activities be captured and logically sequenced, that resources and durations be assigned, that the schedule be traceable horizontally and vertically, that the critical path be valid and total float reasonable. These are structural obligations, distinct from the content of any single intention.

layers.name: Dependency and Constraint Network
layers.description: Logical ordering between planned items, externally imposed date constraints, and the checks that decide whether the network is sound.

findings.name: Ordering dependency and lag
findings.description: The directed relations that sequence planned items, their type, lag and justification.

questions.text: Which ordering relation holds between predecessor and successor: finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish or start-to-finish?
What lag or lead applies, in which duration kind, and what justifies it?
answer_data: Calendar used to apply the lag

questions.text: What physical or contractual reason justifies the dependency rather than mere convenience?
Which dependencies cross the plan boundary to another party's plan?

data_elements.name: predecessorRef
data_elements.description: Preceding planned item in an ordering relation.

data_elements.name: successorRef
data_elements.description: Following planned item in an ordering relation.

data_elements.name: dependencyType
data_elements.description: Ordering relation type between the two items.

data_elements.name: lagDuration
data_elements.description: Signed lag or lead applied to the relation.

data_elements.name: dependencyScope
data_elements.description: Whether the dependency is internal to the plan or crosses to an external party.

artifacts.name: Dependency network
artifacts.description: The directed acyclic set of ordering relations with types, lags and rationale, from which schedule dates are computed.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Plan identifier plus revision counter for the network as a whole; each edge is identified by predecessor identifier, successor identifier and dependency type.

findings.name: Date constraint and scheduling flexibility
findings.description: Externally imposed date constraints on an entry and how far the entry may move without breaching them.

questions.text: Which date constraint is imposed on this entry, and who imposed it?
How flexible is the entry: fixed, movable within a window, or freely schedulable?
When a hard constraint conflicts with network logic, which is honoured and how is the conflict surfaced?
Is the deadline self-imposed, contractual or regulatory?

data_elements.name: dateConstraintType
data_elements.description: Type of imposed date constraint, such as start-no-earlier-than or finish-no-later-than.

data_elements.name: dateConstraintValue
data_elements.description: The constraining date or instant.

data_elements.name: flexibilityClass
data_elements.description: How far the entry may move without approval.

data_elements.name: dateConstraintBasis
data_elements.description: Whether the constraint is self-imposed, contractual or regulatory.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Date constraints and flexibility are attributes of the schedule entry itself, not a separable deliverable. Both iCalendar and JSCalendar express them as properties of the calendar component, and materializing a separate constraint artifact would create a second place where the same date is asserted, which is precisely the duplication that GAO's traceability practice warns against. They are therefore inline data validated together with the entry, and the governing instrument behind a contractual or regulatory deadline is referenced rather than copied.

findings.name: Schedule integrity and quality assessment
findings.description: Structural checks that decide whether a schedule is complete, well-constructed and credible enough to be relied on.

questions.text: Does the schedule capture every activity needed to meet the objective, including work performed by other parties?
Which activities have missing predecessors or successors, negative lag, or excessive use of hard constraints?
Can the schedule be traced horizontally across dependent activities and vertically to its summary levels?
Which health metrics are computed, at what thresholds, and against which scheduling run?

data_elements.name: integrityCheckResult
data_elements.description: Named check with its threshold, computed value and outcome.

data_elements.name: openEndCount
data_elements.description: Number of activities lacking a predecessor or successor.

data_elements.name: traceabilityStatus
data_elements.description: Result of horizontal and vertical traceability verification.

data_elements.name: assessmentObservedAt
data_elements.description: Time the assessment was performed, distinct from the plan revision's modification time.

artifacts.name: Schedule health assessment
artifacts.description: Evidence record of integrity and quality checks against a named plan revision, usable as a gate on baseline approval.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Plan identifier plus assessed revision counter plus zero-padded assessment sequence; the assessment timestamp is an attribute of the record.

findings.name: Precedence network and hierarchical composition
findings.description: RFC 9253 extends RELATED-TO with temporal RELTYPE values FINISHTOSTART, FINISHTOFINISH, STARTTOFINISH and STARTTOSTART, plus GAP for lag (positive) or lead (negative) duration, and FIRST, NEXT, DEPENDS-ON, PARENT, CHILD and SIBLING. P-Plan isPreceededBy is a transitive step ordering without lag types. OWL-Time intervalBefore, intervalMeets, intervalOverlaps and related Allen relations describe interval topology but are not project-management lag. FHIR CarePlan.partOf, basedOn and replaces relate plan instances. REFID groups components without adding meaning. These relation families must be stored distinctly; isPreceededBy is not equivalent to FINISHTOSTART with lag.

data_elements.name: predecessor_id
data_elements.description: Planned item that constrains another.

data_elements.name: successor_id
data_elements.description: Planned item being constrained.

data_elements.name: reltype
data_elements.description: finishtostart, finishtofinish, starttofinish, starttostart, depends-on, parent, child, sibling, first, next, part-of, based-on, replaces.

data_elements.name: gap
data_elements.description: Lead (negative) or lag (positive) between predecessor and successor.

data_elements.name: group_refid
data_elements.description: Shared grouping key with no additional semantics.

data_elements.name: link_uri
data_elements.description: RFC 9253 LINK to an external related resource.

artifacts.name: Dependency record
artifacts.description: Typed relationship between planned items, including precedence type, gap and optional grouping key.
media_or_form: iCalendar RELATED-TO with RELTYPE and GAP
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by predecessor identifier, successor identifier and relation type; relation families are stored distinctly rather than collapsed together.

questions.text: What ordering constraint holds between these planned items, including precedence type and lead or lag gap?
Is this plan or item part of, based on, replacing, parent of or child of another plan, and what grouping REFID if any associates peers?
Independently of project lag, which Allen interval relation holds between the scheduled intervals of the two items?
Does this relationship currently dangle because the target was deleted or cancelled, as RFC 9253 warns for FIRST, NEXT and temporal links?

layers.name: Computation and Resources
layers.description: Dates derived from logic, durations and constraints, and the resources whose availability makes them feasible.

findings.name: Critical path and float computation
findings.description: Separates asserted inputs from computed outputs and records the run that produced the dates, float and critical path.

questions.text: Which dates are asserted inputs and which are computed outputs of a scheduling run?
Which continuous path of activities determines the finish date, and how was its validity checked?
What total float and free float does each activity carry, and what threshold counts as unreasonable?
What triggers recomputation, and is the previous computed result retained?

data_elements.name: computedLateFinish

findings.name: Resource assignment and contention
findings.description: Which agents and resources are assigned at what allocation, their availability, and where they are over-committed.

questions.text: Which agent or resource is assigned to the planned action, in which role and at what allocation?
What availability calendar limits the assigned resource?
Where is the same resource committed to overlapping entries, and how is that resolved?
Which activities carry a duration but no assigned resource, and is that deliberate?

bundles.name: Commitment and Coordination
bundles.description: Intentions that bind an agent to another party, and the negotiation by which times and participation are agreed.
bundles.rationale: ODRL supplies a normative model of duties within an agreement between assigner and assignee, with consequences and remedies; iTIP supplies normative participation states, counter-proposals and organizer authority. Together they show that binding and negotiation are distinct from mere intention.

layers.name: Commitment and Obligation

findings.name: Commitment parties and terms
findings.description: The subset of intentions that bind an agent toward a named beneficiary, with terms and qualifying conditions.

questions.text: Which party issues the commitment and which party is its beneficiary?
What exactly is promised, by when, and under which qualifying conditions?
Is the commitment informal, contractual or regulatory, and what evidence establishes it?
Who is entitled to verify the commitment's existence and terms?

data_elements.description: Beneficiary of the commitment.

findings.name: Remedy, consequence and release
findings.description: What follows non-fulfilment of a commitment, and how commitments are honoured, released or transferred.

questions.text: Which additional duty is triggered when the commitment is not fulfilled?
Which observable event constitutes non-fulfilment, and at what moment is it evaluated?
How is a commitment released, renegotiated or transferred, and whose consent is required?
What evidence closes the commitment as honoured?

artifacts.description: Record of how a commitment ended: honoured with evidence, breached with consequence applied, released or transferred with consent.

layers.name: Participation and Negotiation
layers.description: Who is invited, what they answered, how clashes are detected and how times are renegotiated.

findings.name: Participant role and response state
findings.description: Roles participants hold on an entry, their current response, and how delegation is represented.

questions.text: In which role does each participant appear on the entry?
What is each participant's current response state, and when was it last updated?
Is a reply expected from this participant, and by when?
When a participant delegates, how are delegator and delegate linked on the entry?

data_elements.name: participationRole
data_elements.description: Role such as chair, required, optional or informational.

data_elements.name: participationStatus

artifacts.description: The set of participants on an entry with roles, response states, reply expectations and delegation links.

findings.name: Conflict detection and rescheduling
findings.description: Whether an entry consumes availability, how clashes are found, and how alternative times are proposed and recorded.

questions.text: Does this entry consume the participant's availability or leave them free?
How are overlapping commitments detected across separate calendars and plans?
How is an alternative time proposed, accepted or declined?
When an entry moves, what records the previous time and the reason?

data_elements.name: conflictDetectionResult
data_elements.description: Detected overlap with the conflicting entry references.

data_elements.name: proposedAlternative
data_elements.description: Counter-proposed time and its proposing party.

data_elements.name: rescheduleReason

artifacts.name: Free/busy projection
artifacts.description: Availability-only view over a bounded horizon, disclosing busy intervals without entry content, used for conflict detection across parties.
media_or_form: free/busy component over a stated interval

findings.name: Scheduling methods and message sequencing
findings.description: iTIP methods are PUBLISH, REQUEST, REPLY, ADD, CANCEL, REFRESH, COUNTER and DECLINECOUNTER. Organizer may send PUBLISH, REQUEST, ADD, CANCEL and DECLINECOUNTER; Attendee may send REPLY, REFRESH, COUNTER and a delegation REQUEST. Correlation keys are UID, RECURRENCE-ID, SEQUENCE and DTSTAMP: higher SEQUENCE obsoletes lower for the same UID and recurrence id; matching SEQUENCE ties break on later DTSTAMP. SEQUENCE MUST increment when Organizer changes DTSTART, DTEND, DURATION, DUE, RRULE, RDATE, EXDATE or STATUS. JSCalendar sequence and method (lowercase iTIP method) carry the same semantics. Out-of-order replies must be discarded using persisted last SEQUENCE and DTSTAMP per attendee.

data_elements.name: method
data_elements.description: publish, request, reply, add, cancel, refresh, counter, declinecounter.

data_elements.name: sequence
data_elements.description: Organizer revision number, starting at 0.

data_elements.name: stamp_time
data_elements.description: DTSTAMP or JSCalendar updated used as sequencing tie-breaker.

data_elements.name: originator_role
data_elements.description: organizer or attendee.

data_elements.name: request_status
data_elements.description: iTIP REQUEST-STATUS machine-readable result.

artifacts.name: Scheduling message
artifacts.description: One iTIP-style method payload correlated by UID, recurrence id, sequence and stamp time.
media_or_form: iTIP method payload (PUBLISH, REQUEST, REPLY, ADD, CANCEL, REFRESH, COUNTER, DECLINECOUNTER)
JSCalendar object carrying method and sequence
artifacts.identity_strategy: Correlated by UID plus recurrence identifier plus SEQUENCE, with the later stamp time breaking equal-sequence ties; a higher sequence obsoletes a lower one for the same pair.

questions.text: Which scheduling method is being applied, who may send it, and is this a new object or a revision of an existing UID?
What SEQUENCE and stamp time identify this revision, and does it obsolete a previously stored component with the same UID and recurrence id?
If a reply arrives with a lower sequence or earlier stamp than the last persisted attendee response, should it be discarded?
What spoofing, unauthorized organizer-replacement or flood controls apply to this scheduling message, as warned in iTIP security considerations?

bundles.name: Revision, Execution and Governance
bundles.description: Baselines and change control, progress and realization, closure, provenance, disclosure, retention and exchange.
bundles.rationale: GAO requires a maintained baseline and updates using actual progress and logic; PROV supplies attribution and derivation; NARA shows that schedule records carry authorized disposition; the calendaring standards define the disclosure and exchange primitives. Divergence between intention and outcome is the payload of this bundle.

layers.name: Baseline and Change Control
layers.description: Frozen reference versions and the controlled record of what changed and why.

findings.description: Immutable frozen versions of a plan against which later performance and variance are measured.

How are multiple concurrent baselines distinguished, and which is current?
How is it proven that a stored baseline has not been altered since freezing?

data_elements.name: baselineApproverRef

data_elements.name: baselineDigest

Who authorized the change, and was downstream notification required?
Which timestamps record when the change was decided, applied and observed by consumers?

layers.name: Progress, Realization and Closure
layers.description: Recorded actuals against plan, the acts that realized intentions, and the terminal states of a plan.

findings.description: Progress recorded against the plan as of a stated status date, and the variance computed against baseline.

questions.text: How is progress expressed, and is the measurement method declared rather than assumed?
answer_data: Method code such as percent complete or remaining duration

questions.text: Which actual start and finish dates are recorded, and are dates later than the status date rejected?
What variance against the baseline is computed, and at which level of the plan?
As of which status date is the progress statement valid, and who asserted it?

findings.name: Realization and fulfilment link
findings.description: How intentions are linked to the acts that fulfilled them, including partial, substituted and unplanned outcomes.

How is partial or substituted fulfilment represented without overwriting the original intention?
How is this plan recorded as the plan an executing agent actually followed?
How are acts that occurred with no corresponding intention represented?

findings.description: The agent and activity that produced a plan version, and the prior plans, templates or forecasts it derives from.

From which prior plan, template or forecast is this plan derived?
Is the planning agent autonomous software, and are its identity and version recorded?
Which upstream instruction or request caused the plan to be created?

functions.description: Bind an intention to a named beneficiary with terms, qualifying conditions and the consequence of non-fulfilment.
preconditions: Both parties resolvable
The underlying planned action exists and is not already closed
effects: Subsequent changes to the committed terms require beneficiary notification and a change-log entry
Breach evaluation point established

functions.description: Apply inbound replies and counter-proposals to an entry and resolve competing revisions deterministically.
inputs: Current revision counter and modification timestamp
outputs: Updated participant roster and response states
preconditions: The applying agent holds write authority over the master object
Inbound items carry the entry identifier and a revision counter
effects: Competing revisions resolved by identifier, then revision counter, then modification timestamp
A later timestamp with a lower counter never wins

functions.description: Capture an immutable, digested snapshot of a plan revision as the reference for later variance measurement.
outputs: Immutable baseline snapshot with content digest
preconditions: Approver holds approval authority
An integrity assessment exists for the revision
effects: Snapshot stored append-only and never edited in place
Variance computation against this baseline enabled

functions.description: Apply a field-scoped patch under optimistic concurrency, with a controlled reason and separated decision, application and observation times.
outputs: Notifications to affected beneficiaries and participants
preconditions: Expected revision counter matches the current counter
Reason code drawn from the registered vocabulary
effects: Counter incremented for material fields only
Committed terms not altered without beneficiary notification
Decision, application and observation times recorded separately

inputs: Actual dates, percent complete or remaining duration
preconditions: A baseline exists where variance is requested
No actual date is later than the status date
effects: Actuals stored alongside the baseline, which is never overwritten
Divergence between intention and outcome preserved as data

preconditions: Access decision resolved with deny-by-default applied
Requested horizon bounded

Reads of full-detail entries by non-owners logged with actor, scope, purpose and timestamp

outputs: Disposition action record or continued retention
preconditions: Open commitments resolved, transferred or explicitly acknowledged as residual
No legal hold in force
effects: Plan sealed against further edits; corrections expressed as a successor plan
Future occurrences cancelled with tombstones retained for the replication horizon
Disposition logged with the authorizing records schedule item

functions.name: Split this-and-future
functions.description: Truncate a recurring master at the previous occurrence and create a new master for future occurrences, linking the objects with first and next relations.
